newsitem.title: USA: TIG sees reserve study completed in Q2.
newsitem.headline: TIG sees reserve study completed in Q2.

text.p: TIG Holdings Inc said it is in the midst of a review of its underwriting, pricing and reserving practices, which it expects to complete in the second quarter.
However, TIG chief executive Jon Rotenstreich last week told shareholders that he does not expect any material impact in the second quarter as a result of the loss reserve review.
Instead, Rotenstreich told shareholders that although the study was not yet complete, early indications suggested that the company's loss reserves were adequate.
But an analyst at Salomon Brothers said Thursday he believes the review could result in a charge of $0.50-$1.00 a share in the second quarter.
In addition, analyst Michael Smith said this could increase future loss ratio assumptions by perhaps another $0.50 a share.

The company, in its quarterly financial filing with federal regulators, said the review was launched by its new chief underwriting officer immediately after she was hired in the fourth quarter of 1996.

"This evaluation is expected to be completed in the second quarter of 1997 in conjunction with routine, semi-annual loss and LAE (loss adjustment expense) reserve reviews for both reinsurance and primary lines," the company said in the report.
In the first quarter of 1996, the company increased loss reserves by $31 million and decided to exit a number of lines of business following a similar review.
The company said estimating reserves always involves a certain amount of uncertainty, and that uncertainty is increased when significant changes occur.

Such changes include changes in production sources for existing lines of business, writings of significant blocks of new business, changes in economic conditions, and changes in state or federal laws and regulations.
"TIG has experienced significant changes in each of these areas during the past several years," the company said.

The company said inherent uncertainties in estimating reserves are greater for reinsurance than for primary insurance and this uncertainty was compounded by the relatively short operating history of TIG Re, which was formed in 1987.
Since mid-1996, TIG Re's paid and reported losses have been higher than anticipated, TIG said in the report.
TIG said that management believes these trends are principally attributable to a change in business mix.

In his comments to shareholders last week, Rotenstreich said any shortfalls at TIG Re will be offset by positives at the primary operation, according to a research report provided by TIG's outside public relations firm.

In addition, Rotenstreich said TIG has a stop-loss reinsurance contract. Thus if a reserve shortfall were to materialize on a gross basis, there would likely be no immediate net reserve impact, according to the report.
However, by using the stop-loss, TIG would be foregoing future investment income.
In addition, unlike some of its competitors TIG did not release reserves from prior periods to maintain its earnings in 1996, the report said.
